source.title: Why Lottery Ticket Wins? A Theoretical Perspective of Sample Complexity on Pruned Neural Networks
source.authors: Shuai Zhang; Meng Wang; Sijia Liu; Pin-Yu Chen; Jin-Jun Xiong

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents review.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments applying gradient-based training to pruned and unpruned networks and compares their learning outcomes, but its real-data experiments report test performance rather than the training classification error in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR-10 and MNIST experiments report test accuracy and test error, not training classification error. The theory and synthetic experiments concern one-hidden-layer regression with Gaussian inputs and an oracle-generated target, so they do not directly test the benchmark training-error claims. Cite-only discussion of prior lottery-ticket results is not extracted as the paper's own result.
record.test_reason: The study cites relevant optimization findings but tests none of V1–V6. Its own results concern pruning, local recovery of a sparse teacher, sample complexity, and test performance. Teacher and learner have equal neuron counts; initialization is restricted near ground truth or supplied by a tensor method. These results do not measure extra-width avoidance of spurious minima, benchmark training classification error, or the depth, initialization, learning-rate, and normalization comparisons specified.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. More precisely, the authors characterize how retained connections affect local convergence, sample complexity, and recovery accuracy in one-hidden-layer Gaussian-input teacher–student networks, and interpret this as justification for winning-ticket generalization. The guarantees require an accurate mask, sufficient samples, and suitable initialization; exact recovery additionally requires noiseless outputs. Experiments extend the pruning observations to inaccurate masks and multilayer benchmark test performance.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies pruning and accelerated gradient descent in an oracle-learner setting, with tensor initialization in theory, GraSP or IMP in experiments, and primarily model-recovery/test-error outcomes rather than the claim's benchmark training-classification-error measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with pruning ratio, sample count, mask accuracy, and re; overly aggressive pruning (greater than 80%) and too few samples (N = 100) leave high synthetic test error.

fits_no_version.finding: With controlled near-oracle initialization, pruning enlarges the empirically successful recovery region and accelerates recovery; AGD converges faster than GD.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested sparse one-hidden-layer ReLU oracle problem, pruning can improve local recovery and convergence speed.

fits_no_version.finding: Synthetic recovery sample requirements depend on r̃, and noisy recovery error increases with sqrt(r̃) and noise level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse teacher recovery depends on the number and arrangement of retained connections, sample count, and measurement noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Appropriate pruning improves test performance or reduces sample requirements; excessive pruning and insufficient samples can yield poor performance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested GraSP and IMP procedures, pruning can improve generalization and sample efficiency within suitable pruning and data ranges.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2021, 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems
record.problems: The CIFAR-10 and MNIST results are reported as test accuracy, not training error, and are presented in figures without exact plotted values in the supplied text. The principal theoretical results assume an accurate mask, one hidden layer, Gaussian inputs, and an oracle-learner regression setup; the authors identify one-hidden-layer and Gaussian-input limitations. Benchmark experiments are representative rather than comprehensive and do not measure the claim's classification training error.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible claim-version rows were identified. All extracted rows concern synthetic oracle-regression recovery or test metrics and are recorded under versions ['none']; none directly measures the claim versions' stated outcomes.

untested.parts: Training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, and the stated size, stopping, and regularization conditions.
Spurious-minimum frequency from standard initialization as teacher/student widths grow, and the effect of adding one or two student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation, identity-shortcut comparisons, and the special-initialization exceptions.
Activation-matched initialization comparisons, signal/gradient propagation, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, and trainable depth.
Training above the initial stability limit, loss transients, sharpness evolution, and divergence thresholds.
Batch-normalization effects on training speed and learning-rate tolerance, and comparison with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6 because their measures do not establish those effects; this does not deny the reported pruning results. No missing result bearing on a specified version was found in the supplied text.

versions.untested_parts: The paper reports no training classification error on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, and does not test random or corrupted labels or the effects of model size, early stopping, or regularization on training error.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student sweep varies student width relative to teacher width or measures spurious local minima.
No comparison of plain versus residual networks by depth or training error; no tests of shortcuts, Fixup, or normalization for the stated depth effects.
No comparison of initialization schemes for signal propagation, training speed, or trainable depth in plain networks.
No learning-rate stability-limit sweep, curvature tracking, or loss-divergence analysis of the kind specified.
No batch-normalization comparison of learning speed or learning-rate tolerance, nor a Fixup comparison.
